newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN ministers to review farm tariff deadlock.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN ministers to review farm tariff deadlock.

text.p: ASEAN economic ministers will try to break a deadlock over a timetable for cutting tariffs on sensitive farm products when they meet this week, sources at a preparatory meeting of senior officials said on Tuesday.
"The issue will go before the ministers," an official said.

He said Indonesia and the Philippines wanted to extend the implementation period for phasing out tariffs on certain farm products -- notably rice and sugar -- as part of the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA).

Economic ministers of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) will review progress in liberalising tariffs on products listed under the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) scheme.
AFTA's aim is to reduce tariffs on goods included in the CEPT to zero-to-five percent by 2003.
The ministers meet on Wednesday as the AFTA council to review progress on tariff reduction and then hold their annual economic meeting on Thursday.
The ministers will debate problems -- such as the deadlock over farm products -- that officials failed to resolve in their preparatory sessions on Monday and Tuesday.
Countries can label as "sensitive" unprocessed farm products regarded as vital to their national welfare but they must eventually be included in the tariff reduction scheme.
Indonesia and the Philippines, however, have baulked at the tariff reduction deadline of 2010. Officials said they wanted to extend the deadline by 10 years.
Indonesia has listed a total of 15 unprocessed agricultural products as sensitive, including soybeans, cloves and wheat.
Other ASEAN members Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei and Vietnam have accepted the earlier deadline.
The ministers will also receive a report from government investment officials on a proposed framework for an ASEAN Investment Area (AFTA) to boost investment within and from outside the region.
ASEAN sources said the ministers were expected to tell experts to fine tune the proposal before an informal summit meeting of ASEAN leaders late in the year.
But officials said ministers would be unable to sign a proposed mechanism for resolving trade disputes within ASEAN because the Vietnamese delegation had failed to arrive with signing authority.
An ASEAN source said the agreement should be in place for the ASEAN summit.
The AFTA council will meet on Wednesday afternoon, followed by a day-long ministerial meeting on Thursday. On Friday, the ministers will meet their counterparts from Australia, New Zealand and Japan.
